headline: Light rain reaches Kentucky tonight before a warm, breezy Tuesday; the Upstate wedge weakens into a dry early-week warm-up
disclaimer: Independent amateur analysis. This is not an official forecast or warning. Follow the National Weather Service and local authorities during hazardous weather.

refresh.workflow: Update and commit forecast.json once. GitHub Actions automatically locks the prior issue in forecast-history.json. Then verify the GitHub Pages URL; every Google Sites embed reads the same file and refreshes automatically.

kentucky.name: Central Kentucky
kentucky.subtitle: Danville primary · Lexington comparison
kentucky.summary: A compact shortwave approaches beneath a broad cloud shield today while the initially dry lower troposphere delays measurable rain around Danville. Isentropic ascent and increasing precipitable water moisten the column from the top downward, allowing light stratiform showers to become more likely this evening and overnight. The wave exits Monday morning, but shallow saturation may preserve low cloud or drizzle before brief ridging and southwest flow promote partial clearing. By Tuesday, strengthening southerly flow ahead of the next front produces a warm and increasingly breezy day; the principal frontal rain arrives near or just beyond the end of this 72-hour window.
kentucky.currentConditions: At 7:35 AM EST, KDVK was 54°F with a 46°F dew point, calm wind, clear sky and visibility above 10 miles. At 6:54 AM, KLEX was 60°F with a 44°F dew point, a light southeast wind and visibility above 10 miles. Neither station reported rain or fog, and no official NWS alert was active for Danville at the final issuance check.

days.label: Sunday
days.precipitation: 15–30% through late afternoon; 50–60% evening and overnight
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Sunday at issuance. Independent concern is limited to wet roads, low ceilings and locally reduced visibility tonight; thunder, severe weather and flooding are not expected.
days.forecast: Cloudy with virga or a few sprinkles possible before measurable light showers become more likely after roughly 4–6 PM. Dry low levels delay the rain despite increasing ascent aloft. The most likely Danville high is near 66°F. Southeast wind runs 3–8 mph with gusts around 12–24 mph. Local rainfall tonight should generally total 0.05–0.20 inch, with an isolated 0.25–0.50 inch wetter-model outcome possible. After the verified KDVK low correction, the most likely overnight low is near 50°F. Patchy fog may mix with low cloud or drizzle late tonight, but dense fog remains unlikely.

days.label: Monday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Monday at issuance. Low cloud, drizzle or a lingering early light shower is possible, but no threshold independent hazard is expected.
days.forecast: Low cloud, patchy fog, drizzle or a lingering light shower tapers during the morning as the shortwave lifts northeast. A brief midlevel ridge and developing southwest flow should allow partial afternoon improvement, although clearing timing is the main temperature uncertainty. The most likely Danville high is near 68°F. Southeast wind becomes south around 5–10 mph with gusts of 18–28 mph. After the verified KDVK low correction, the most likely Monday-night low is near 53°F.

days.label: Tuesday
days.precipitation: 5% or less through evening; 25–35% after about 1 AM Wednesday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Tuesday at issuance. Independent concern is an increasingly breezy south wind with gusts around 22–33 mph; the approaching frontal rain should begin near the end of the validity window.
days.forecast: Mostly sunny to partly cloudy, warm and increasingly breezy beneath shortwave ridging and strengthening low-level warm advection. The most likely Danville high is near 75°F. South wind increases to 8–14 mph with gusts around 22–33 mph later in the day and evening. After the verified KDVK low correction, the most likely Tuesday-night low is near 59°F. Clouds thicken overnight, with showers beginning after about 1 AM Wednesday as the front approaches.

kentucky.bottomLine: Danville stays mostly dry through much of Sunday before light showers become more likely this evening and tonight, generally producing 0.05–0.20 inch. Lingering low cloud, patchy fog or drizzle tapers Monday, then Tuesday turns warm and increasingly breezy ahead of the next front. Bias-corrected most likely Danville highs are 66°F, 68°F and 75°F; most likely lows are 50°F, 53°F and 59°F.
kentucky.confidence: Moderate-high on Sunday temperature; moderate on Sunday-evening rain timing and amount; moderate on Monday clearing; high on Tuesday warmth and moderate on late-night frontal timing

upstate.name: Upstate South Carolina
upstate.subtitle: Clemson primary · Central/Pickens County comparison
upstate.summary: A weakening Appalachian cold-air-damming wedge and roughly 1030-mb parent high maintain shallow cool northeast flow and extensive cloud today. Weak isentropic ascent has produced only intermittent drizzle or very light rain because much of the deeper moisture and lift remain west and southwest over north Georgia and the Tennessee Valley. The parent high shifts toward the western Atlantic tonight, shutting down the upglide and allowing the wedge to erode through Monday. By Tuesday, deeper mixing beneath a weak ridge supports a dry return to the lower 70s, while the next organized rain remains beyond the forecast window.
upstate.currentConditions: At 6:54 AM EST, KCEU was 56°F with a 45°F dew point, northeast wind near 5 mph, visibility above 10 miles and overcast cloud near 11,000 feet; 0.01 inch had fallen and earlier light rain had ended. At 7:35 AM, KLQK was 56°F with a 44°F dew point, east-northeast wind near 5 mph, visibility above 10 miles and overcast cloud near 12,000 feet; its remark reported distant lightning west. That distant observation does not outweigh the otherwise negligible local instability and thunder signal. No official NWS alert was active for Clemson or Central. Tempest data was not used.

days.label: Sunday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Sunday at issuance. Independent concerns are brief drizzle or light rain and a sub-advisory northeast breeze; thunder, flooding and severe weather are not expected.
days.forecast: Cloudy and cool beneath the weakening wedge. Intermittent drizzle or light rain early should diminish as the weak upglide shifts away; most locations receive only a trace to 0.05 inch, although an isolated total near 0.10 inch is possible. The most likely high is near 63°F. Northeast wind runs 8–13 mph with gusts around 20–25 mph. Applying the station corrections, the most likely Clemson low is near 54°F and Central/Pickens is near 50°F. Significant fog is unlikely in the continued mixing and cloud.

days.label: Monday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Monday at issuance. No threshold independent hazard is expected; the main uncertainty is how quickly residual cloud and the shallow cool pool erode.
days.forecast: Residual northeast flow and cloud may linger early, then the parent high shifts offshore and daytime mixing gradually erodes the shallow wedge. Partly to mostly sunny conditions should develop. The most likely Clemson/Central high is near 69°F. East-northeast wind runs 6–10 mph with occasional gusts around 15–20 mph. Applying the station corrections, the most likely Clemson low is near 55°F and Central/Pickens is near 51°F. The day should remain measurable-rain free.

days.label: Tuesday
days.hazard: No official NWS alert is active for Tuesday at issuance. No threshold independent hazard is expected; a colder slow-wedge-erosion NAM outcome remains a lower-probability temperature risk.
days.forecast: Mostly sunny before high cloud increases late. With the wedge removed, deeper boundary-layer mixing beneath weak ridging supports a most likely high near 73°F. East-northeast wind runs 6–10 mph with gusts generally 12–18 mph. Applying the station corrections, the most likely Clemson low is near 59°F and Central/Pickens is near 55°F. Organized ascent remains absent through Tuesday evening, so appreciable rain waits until Wednesday beyond the validity window.

upstate.bottomLine: Brief drizzle or light rain fades today while the weakening wedge keeps the Upstate cloudy, cool and breezy. The wedge erodes Monday and should be gone Tuesday, supporting a dry warm-up from near 63°F today to about 69°F Monday and 73°F Tuesday. Bias-corrected Clemson lows are near 54°F, 55°F and 59°F, with colder Central/Pickens values near 50°F, 51°F and 55°F.
upstate.confidence: High that any Sunday rain remains light; moderate-high on the dry Monday-Tuesday forecast; moderate on wedge-erosion timing and Tuesday temperature

analysisLinks.label: College of DuPage satellite and radar

sourceNotes: No official NWS alert was active for the Danville, Clemson or Central point at the final issuance checks. Official NWS alerts remain explicitly separate from this independent analysis.

The latest KDVK, KLEX, KCEU and KLQK observations were consulted. Kentucky stations were rain-free, with KDVK clear and KLEX beneath only a few midlevel clouds. KCEU and KLQK were overcast in northeast flow after intermittent light rain or drizzle, with 0.01 inch measured at KCEU. KLQK reported distant lightning west at 12:35Z; it was treated as an observation outside the immediate point rather than evidence of a local thunder threat because official guidance and fresh profiles retain negligible instability. These observations support delayed top-down saturation in Kentucky and a still-present but weakening Upstate wedge.

The 11:08Z Louisville discussion supports dry low levels through much of Sunday, light rain reaching the Bluegrass during the evening, one tenth inch or less locally, and low cloud or drizzle lingering into Monday morning. The 10:23Z Greenville-Spartanburg discussion supports a weakening cold-air-damming wedge, only sprinkles or a few hundredths today, dry Monday and Tuesday, and complete wedge erosion by Tuesday.

College of DuPage 11:50–11:55Z radar showed the organized rain shield west and southwest of the Bluegrass and Upstate, with only spotty light precipitation near Clemson. The 11:51:17Z infrared frames showed broad layered cloud over both regions but the deeper, colder cloud mass displaced west and south.

Chris Bailey's exact November 1 Kentucky Weather Center post, ‘November Looks Like a Very Active Month,’ and its NAM 3-km future-radar graphic were consulted as accepted source material. Bailey brings showers into western Kentucky Sunday morning, expands them east and northeast Sunday evening and night, tapers leftovers Monday, and describes Election Day as warm and breezy. Details absent from the post or unreadable in its graphic were not inferred.

Bailey's local 0.50–1.00-inch possibility for western and central Kentucky, with much lighter totals farther east, and the Louisville office's Bluegrass-specific one-tenth-inch-or-less forecast are reconciled by the explicitly strong west-to-east rainfall gradient. Danville is forecast on the lighter eastern side, with 0.05–0.20 inch most likely and an isolated 0.25–0.50 inch wetter-model outcome possible.

The fresh Danville point forecast gives 67°F Sunday, 70°F Monday and 77°F Tuesday. Accuracy-calibrated regional ranges are 64–69°F, 64–69°F and 72–78°F, while the prose supplies narrower bias-corrected Danville most-likely values of 66°F, 68°F and 75°F. The Tuesday value was lowered one degree after the fresh local GRIB package placed its four-model KDVK median near 74°F before the −1°F station correction.

Kentucky precipitation guidance differs materially on amount: BUFKIT GFS and NAM 3-km are light; NAM, RRFS and some HiResW solutions are wetter; SREF has a 0.17-inch median and a 0.06–0.46-inch interquartile range. The fresh local GRIB package has only two valid daily-QPF contributors at KDVK, with HRRR at 0.01 inch and RAP at 0.51 inch. The NWS gradient, radar and dry sub-cloud layer support a delayed Sunday-evening onset and 0.05–0.20 inch most likely, while an isolated 0.25–0.50 inch wetter-model outcome is retained rather than discarded.

Upstate official and model guidance clusters Sunday's high near 61–64°F, Monday near the upper 60s and Tuesday around the lower 70s. The NAM Tuesday value near 60°F is retained as a lower-probability slow-wedge-erosion tail because it conflicts with the NWS point forecast, GFS, ECMWF and GEFS mean.

The Upstate ECMWF is a wetter Sunday outlier near 0.22 inch. Its value and the GEFS probability summarize the full calendar-day period and include rain or drizzle already observed before this forecast was issued. For the remaining period, current observations, radar, the GSP discussion and GFS/NAM/HRRR/RAP favor only a trace to 0.05 inch for most locations, while an isolated total near 0.10 inch remains possible.

Fresh KGSP BUFKIT proxy profiles keep CAPE essentially zero and precipitable water near 1.0–1.1 inches today. These regional proxies are not exact KCEU or KLQK profiles; they support cloud, drizzle and light rain without thunder or convective downpours.

Atmospheric evolution — Central Kentucky: midlevel cloud and ascent arrive before the dry lower troposphere saturates, so early echoes can evaporate as virga. Fresh KDVK GRIB profiles place Sunday 850-mb temperature near 9–10°C, 700-mb humidity near a 91% median, precipitable water at 1.23–1.35 inches and median 850-mb wind near 40 mph, with negative vertical motion indicating ascent. This supports top-down moistening, light stratiform rain, gusts above the earlier draft and patchy fog or reduced visibility overnight. Monday profiles warm to an 11.6°C median at 850 mb while 500-mb heights rise by about 11 m and median 700-mb humidity remains near 78%, supporting a shower/drizzle taper but uncertain cloud erosion. Tuesday profiles warm to about 12.6°C at 850 mb while median 850-mb wind strengthens to about 46 mph and 500-mb heights fall roughly 47 m, producing warm, breezy pre-frontal flow before the next rain approaches overnight.

Atmospheric evolution — Upstate: a weakening 1030-mb parent high maintains shallow northeast flow and a stable terrain-anchored cool layer today while weak upglide produces only intermittent drizzle. As the high shifts toward the western Atlantic tonight, the pressure pattern becomes less favorable for damming. Daytime mixing erodes the residual wedge Monday, and deeper mixing beneath weak ridging supports a dry lower-70s Tuesday.

The locally extracted Kentucky package was generated at 2026-11-01T12:43:28Z from 9,062 decoded GRIB messages, 234 reduced records and 36 station-day benchmarks. All seven requested model families are present. The 06Z ECMWF, GEFS, GFS and NAM extend 78 hours; 06Z HRRR ends at 48 hours, 06Z NAM 3-km at 60 hours and 09Z RAP at 51 hours. Partial horizons are disclosed and no model is extrapolated.

Fresh GRIB surface reconciliation at KDVK: Sunday high/low spans 62.4–70.6°F and 50.7–56.6°F with medians 66.0°F and 52.4°F; Monday spans 60.3–73.2°F and 51.0–57.0°F with medians 68.4°F and 54.3°F; Tuesday's four-model high spans 71.8–76.6°F with a 74.0°F median. Median daily maximum gusts are 22.4, 24.6 and 27.4 mph, and Tuesday reaches 33.2 mph in the upper model envelope. KDVK low corrections convert the first two raw median lows to about 50°F and 52°F; NWS and BUFKIT evidence supports the stated 53°F Monday-night value and 59°F Tuesday-night value where the local daily summary has no complete Tuesday low.

Fresh Warehouse and Iowa State KGSP profiles were used only as an Upstate regional proxy, not as an exact KCEU or KLQK profile. BUFKIT is a profile and visualization interface for underlying model cycles, not an additional independent model.
The latest cumulative accuracy summary was consulted: 103 of 114 checkpoints are verified and all-category accuracy is 79.9% overall, including 83.9% for Central Kentucky and 75.9% for the Upstate.

Current KDVK, KCEU and KLQK station corrections, empirical lead-specific temperature widths, regime-specific model weights, explicit precipitation and wind windows, measurable wind ranges and official-alert separation were applied. The current corrections are KDVK high −1°F, KDVK low −2°F, KCEU low +2°F and KLQK low −3.5°F.

The low-PoP reliability bin remains underforecast: forecasts averaging 5.4% have observed occurrence of 18.0%. Small shower and drizzle risks were therefore retained rather than reflexively suppressed.

Temperature cards retain calibrated regional coverage widths, while prose gives narrower most-likely Danville, Clemson and Central point values. The overnight ranges represent verified station and terrain spread, not uncertainty at one exact point.
